title: How Much You Should Have Saved by Age 30, 40, 50, and 60 for Retirement
description: Benchmarking your progress against Fidelity's 'Salary Multiplier' guidelines.
content:
One of the hardest parts of retirement planning is knowing if you are 'on track.' A dollar amount (like $500k) doesn't tell the whole story because lifestyle costs vary. Financial institutions like Fidelity have developed 'Salary Multipliers'—benchmarks based on your age and income—that act as a better yardstick. These milestones help you self-audit your progress and adjust your savings rate before it is too late.

Key Takeaways

  • The '1x' Rule: By age 30, you should have 1x your annual salary saved. (e.g., Salary $70k -> Savings $70k).
  • The Acceleration: By age 40, aim for 3x. By age 50, aim for 6x. By age 67, aim for 10x.
  • Income Changes: If your salary doubles at age 39, you will suddenly look 'behind.' Don't panic. Use the higher income to catch up, but remember you might not need 10x of your peak salary, just 10x of your spending.
  • Net Worth vs. Invested Assets: These benchmarks generally refer to invested retirement assets, not home equity. You can't eat your house.

Why It Matters (US Context)

These benchmarks assume you want to maintain your current lifestyle in retirement and retire at age 67. If you want to retire early (FIRE) or live luxuriously, you need to hit these numbers ~10 years earlier.

The Checkpoints

Are you ahead or behind?

Age 30: 1x Salary

Goal: Establish the habit.
Example: Earning $60k. Saved $60k.
Reality: Hard for those with student loans. If you are at 0.5x, ramp up contributions to 15%.

Age 40: 3x Salary

Goal: Compound interest takes over.
Example: Earning $100k. Saved $300k.
Critical Phase: This is where you see separation. If you are at 1x here, you need to save aggressive amounts (25%+) to catch up.

Age 50: 6x Salary

Goal: Peak earning accumulation.
Example: Earning $120k. Saved $720k.
Catch-Up: IRS allows extra contributions ($7,500) starting now. Use them.

Age 60: 8x Salary

Goal: Safety and preservation.
Example: Earning $130k. Saved $1.04M.
Asset Allocation: Start shifting slightly to bonds to protect the pile.

What to Do if You Are Behind

  1. Don't Anchor to Salary: If you make $200k but live on $50k, you don't need 10x $200k ($2M). You need 25x your spending ($1.25M). Calculate based on expenses, not income.
  2. Work Longer: Delaying retirement from 67 to 70 is the ultimate cheat code. It increases Social Security by ~24% and reduces the portfolio size needed by ~20%.
  3. Downsize: If you house-hack or move to a cheaper state in retirement, your 'Replacement Income' need drops. A 10x shortfall becomes a 15x surplus if expenses drop 40%.
  4. The 'Super-Save' Decade: Your 50s are often the best time to save (kids gone, mortgage low). You can save 40% of income and catch up rapidly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Social Security count?

These benchmarks assume you get Social Security. Without SS, you would need closer to 15x-20x salary to self-fund 100%.

What about pensions?

A pension counts as savings. Calculate the 'Lump Sum' value or subtract the pension income from your spending needs. A $40k pension reduces your required nest egg by $1 Million.

Is 10x enough?

It replaces ~45% of your pre-retirement income. Added to Social Security (~35%), you replace ~80%. Since you no longer save for retirement or pay FICA taxes, 80% usually feels like 100%.
